Canada, lumber companies seek USMCA reviews against 2024 U.S. lumber duties
November 25, 2026 | 8:42 am CST
Canada, lumber companies seek USMCA reviews against 2024 U.S. lumber duties

OTTAWA & WASHINGTON, D.C. — Canada, provincial governments and a group of Canadian lumber producers have initiated two new challenges to US softwood lumber trade-duty decisions. Notices published in the US Federal Register confirm requests for review by binational panels under Article 10.12 of the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA).

Initiated Nov. 18, Canada and the lumber producers seek reviews of the U.S. Department of Commerce's 2024 administrative reviews of the duties. The proceedings address two separate issues: antidumping duties, which are intended to counter imports sold below fair market value, and countervailing duties, which address alleged government subsidies.

Notices published in the Federal Register on Nov. 23 confirmed that the challenges involve Canadian federal and provincial governments, along with several major lumber producers. Among the companies identified are Canfor, Interfor, Tolko, West Fraser and J.D. Irving.
Two separate panel matters cover the 2024 antidumping and countervailing-duty reviews.
The applications were filed on 18 November; official notices appeared on 23 November.
The antidumping case is numbered USA–CDA–2026–10.12–02; the countervailing-duty case is USA–CDA–2026–10.12–01.
The notices do not suspend collection of duties or announce revised rates.

The countervailing-duty case is identified in the US Secretariat notice as USA–CDA–2026–10.12–01. Its requests were made by the Government of Canada and several provincial governments, industry councils and named producers, as well as other interested parties. The antidumping case, USA–CDA–2026–10.12–02, also includes requests from companies and industry groups affected by the review results.

Although both matters concern Canadian softwood lumber, antidumping and countervailing duties are legally distinct. The former relates to dumping determinations; the latter concerns alleged subsidies. A development in one case should not be described as changing the outcome of the other.

The USMCA provides a binational panel review process through which companies and governments can challenge certain trade determinations made by the U.S. Department of Commerce. The panels examine whether the department's decisions comply with applicable trade laws.

The dispute remains significant for Canada's forest products sector, which relies heavily on exports to the U.S. Natural Resources Canada has identified the U.S. as the destination for a substantial share of Canadian softwood lumber production, leaving producers exposed to changes in U.S. trade policy and duties.

The new filings represent another step in the ongoing dispute, rather than an immediate change to the duties currently applied to Canadian lumber imports. The panel reviews will determine whether the challenged administrative review results should stand.
